questions.q: Walk one request from DNS to the database and back. Where does each millisecond go?
also: How does a request flow end-to-end through a production system?
a: Name every hop: DNS, TLS, CDN or edge, load balancer, service, cache, database. Give each hop a latency budget, then say which hops dominate p99 and why.
DNS, edge or CDN, load balancer, gateway, service, cache, datastore, and back. State what each hop does, what can fail there, and where latency accumulates.

questions.q: Read traffic grows 10x in one quarter. What do you change first, and what do you refuse to change?
also: How do I design a service that can handle 10x more traffic with minimal changes?
a: Measure the bottleneck before acting. Cache and add read replicas before sharding. Hold the API contract and data model steady so clients and teams do not have to move.
Stateless services behind a load balancer, caching for hot reads, replicas, partitionable data, and autoscaling with tested limits. Find the first bottleneck by load testing, not guessing.

questions.q: Choose a load balancing strategy for long-lived connections versus short RPCs.
a: Round robin, least-request, power of two choices, consistent hashing. Connection draining, slow start for new instances, and what happens to sticky state on scale-in.

questions.q: Size a system for 50,000 requests per second with a 100 ms hard deadline.
a: Back-of-envelope CPU, memory and network per request. Fan-out cost, timeout budget split across calls, 30 to 40 percent headroom, and what you drop when the deadline is about to be missed.

questions.q: What are the trade-offs between vertical and horizontal scaling?
a: Vertical is simple and has a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal needs statelessness or partitioning, adds coordination cost, and scales further. Most systems do vertical first, then horizontal where the data allows.

questions.q: When does splitting a monolith pay for itself?
also: How do I decide when to split a monolith into services?
a: Team ownership lines, different deploy cadence, different scaling profiles. Price in the costs: network failure modes, distributed data, on-call load. A modular monolith is a valid answer.
Split along team and data ownership lines when deploy independence or scaling needs diverge. Cost: network failures, distributed data, operational load. A modular monolith may be enough.

questions.q: Design admission control so a service stays up through a 20x spike.
also: How do I protect downstream services from traffic spikes?
a: Shed by priority, bound every queue, use adaptive concurrency limits, apply per-tenant quotas, and fail fast with Retry-After. Protect the critical path first, batch work last.
Rate limits and concurrency caps at the caller, queues that smooth bursts, circuit breakers, load shedding by priority, and caching in front of the dependency.

questions.q: How do I design for backpressure in a high-traffic system?
a: Bounded queues, propagate pressure upstream (blocking, credits, 429s), shed load deliberately, and size consumers to drain bursts. Unbounded buffers only move the failure later.

questions.q: How do I choose between synchronous and asynchronous communication?
a: Synchronous when the caller needs the answer to proceed and latency is bounded. Asynchronous to decouple availability, absorb bursts and run slow work. Cost of async: eventual results, retries, duplicate handling.

questions.q: When should I use a queue versus direct RPC?
a: Queue for buffering, fan-out, retries and independent consumer speed. RPC for request-scoped answers with a tight deadline. Never put a queue in a path that needs a synchronous response without a reply mechanism.

questions.q: Where is the boundary between OLTP and OLAP, and how does data cross it?
a: Row store for transactions, columnar store for analytics. Move data by change data capture, not dual writes. Cover lag, backfill, and schema drift between the two sides.

questions.q: How do I decide between SQL, NoSQL, and search engines?
a: Start from access patterns and consistency needs. Relational for transactions and ad hoc queries, key-value or wide-column for known-key scale, search engines for text and faceting as a derived index, never the source of truth.

questions.q: How do I model data differently for OLTP versus OLAP workloads?
a: OLTP: normalized rows, narrow transactions, point lookups. OLAP: denormalized wide tables or star schemas in columnar storage, loaded from OLTP by change data capture or batch.

questions.q: Pick a partition key for a multi-tenant ledger, then show how it fails.
also: What does a good partition key look like in a distributed store?
a: Tenant, account or time as candidates. Failure cases: one giant tenant, time-based hot tail, cross-partition queries. Mitigate with composite keys, salting for heavy keys, and a resharding plan.
High cardinality, even access, aligned with the dominant query, and stable over time. Avoid monotonically increasing keys that create a hot tail.

questions.q: A hot partition shows up at 2 a.m. Diagnose it and fix it without downtime.
also: How do I avoid hot partitions and skew?
a: Confirm skew from per-partition metrics. Short-term: cache the hot key, rate limit, split the range. Long-term: change the key, add a salt, rebalance online. Say how you verify the fix.
Choose a well-distributed key, salt or split heavy keys, cache hot reads, and monitor per-partition load so skew is seen before it becomes an outage.

questions.q: How do I shard data by user, tenant, region, or something else?
a: Shard on the dimension most queries filter by and that spreads load evenly. Cover cross-shard queries, rebalancing, and tenant or region affinity for locality and compliance.

questions.q: Your data is sharded by user id, but you need to query by email or by order status. How do secondary indexes work in a sharded store?
a: Secondary indexes in a sharded system are either local to each shard (cheap writes, scatter-gather reads) or global and partitioned by the indexed value (single-shard reads, cross-shard writes that are typically asynchronous). Choose by query frequency and how fresh the index must be.

questions.q: Design indexes for a table that takes 90 percent writes.
also: How should I index for read-heavy versus write-heavy workloads?
a: Every index taxes writes. Keep the few that serve real queries, prefer covering indexes, consider LSM engines, and push ad hoc reads to a replica or search store.
Read-heavy: more indexes, covering indexes, materialized views. Write-heavy: few indexes, append-friendly storage, deferred or asynchronous secondary structures.

questions.q: Migrate a billion-row table to a new schema with zero downtime.
also: How do I design a migration strategy for a huge table?
a: Expand, dual write, throttled backfill, verify with checksums, shadow reads, cut over, then contract. Keep a rollback path until the old column has been unused for a full cycle.
Expand and contract with dual writes, a throttled resumable backfill, verification before cutover, a rollback window, and cleanup only after the old path is provably idle.

questions.q: How do I safely backfill data in production?
a: Throttle against production load, make the job idempotent and resumable, process in key ranges, verify with counts and checksums, and keep it observable and stoppable.

questions.q: How do I do schema changes without downtime?
a: Expand and contract: add nullable, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, remove the old. Avoid long locks and test the online DDL path against production-size data.

questions.q: Design retention, soft delete and legal erasure so they do not contradict each other.
also: How do I design soft delete, archival, and retention?
a: Different clocks for each: soft delete for undo, retention for policy, erasure for law. Cover backups, derived stores, logs, and how you prove deletion happened.
Deleted flag or tombstone for undo, tiered storage for old data, retention policies with automated purge, and explicit handling for legal deletion and backups.

questions.q: How do I handle multi-tenant data isolation?
a: Row-level with tenant id on every query and enforced in the data layer, schema per tenant, or database per tenant. Trade isolation strength against cost and operational load. Plan noisy-neighbor controls and tenant export.

questions.q: Your database runs at read committed. Which bugs can that cause, and when do you need something stronger?
a: Isolation level decides which concurrency anomalies the database prevents for you. Most databases default to read committed, which still allows lost updates and write skew, so you must know which invariants need atomic updates, row locks, constraints or serializable isolation.

questions.q: Optimistic or pessimistic concurrency control: how do you choose, and what breaks with each?
a: Optimistic control lets everyone proceed and detects conflicts at write time (a version check); pessimistic control locks first so conflicts can't happen. Choose by conflict rate, cost of retrying, and how long the critical section is.

questions.q: Leader-follower, multi-leader or leaderless replication: what does each cost you, and which would you pick?
a: Single-leader replication is simplest and gives one order of writes, at the cost of a write bottleneck and failover risk. Multi-leader allows writes in several places but requires conflict resolution. Leaderless (quorum) replication tolerates node failures without failover but needs careful quorum and repair design.

questions.q: Design uploads of multi-gigabyte files from users with unreliable connections.
a: Keep large bytes off your application servers. Clients upload directly to object storage using short-lived presigned URLs, in parts that can be retried and resumed, and your system tracks the upload as a resource with states, processing it asynchronously once complete.

questions.q: Count unique visitors and top-K items across billions of events per day. Do you need exact answers?
a: When the question is 'about how many' or 'which are the biggest', probabilistic structures give small, mergeable answers with bounded error: HyperLogLog for distinct counts, count-min sketch and heavy-hitter algorithms for frequencies and top-K, Bloom filters for membership. Use exact counting only where correctness matters.

questions.q: Find the nearest drivers, stores or users to a location quickly. How do you index location data?
a: Spatial queries need a spatial index that groups nearby points: geohash prefixes, quadtrees, Google S2 or Uber H3 cells, or R-trees (PostGIS). Query the relevant cells and neighbours to get candidates, then rank by exact distance. Fast-moving points need an in-memory, frequently updated index.

questions.q: Where should I cache: client, edge, service, or DB layer?
a: Closer to the user means lower latency and weaker control over invalidation. Match the layer to data volatility and sharing: edge for public static, service for computed results, DB layer for hot rows.

questions.q: How do I pick between write-through, write-back, and write-around caching?
a: Write-through keeps cache and store aligned at write cost. Write-back is fast but risks loss on cache failure. Write-around avoids polluting the cache with data that is rarely read.

questions.q: How do I design cache invalidation rules that do not become a nightmare?
a: Prefer TTLs with jitter plus event-driven invalidation for the few cases that need it. Version keys instead of deleting, keep key construction in one place, and accept bounded staleness explicitly.

questions.q: How do I handle cache stampede and thundering herd?
a: Request coalescing so one caller rebuilds, stale-while-revalidate, TTL jitter, early refresh, and a lock or lease with a short timeout.

questions.q: What is my caching story for hot keys and large objects?
a: Replicate hot keys across nodes or add a local near-cache, split large values, compress, and cap object size. Watch for one key saturating one cache shard.

questions.q: How do I measure whether a cache is actually helping?
a: Hit ratio by key class, latency with and without, origin load saved, eviction rate, and cost per hit. A high hit ratio on cheap reads can still be pointless.

questions.q: Your Redis cache cluster goes down at peak. What happens, and how should the system behave?
a: A cache that absorbs most reads is load-bearing infrastructure. When it fails, uncontrolled fall-through can take down the database. Design the failure mode: replication for the cache, bounded fall-through, degraded responses, and careful recovery with warming.

questions.q: How do you size a cache and choose an eviction policy?
a: Size a cache to hold the working set (the keys reused within their useful lifetime), using the hit-ratio curve to find diminishing returns. Choose eviction by access pattern: LRU for recency, LFU for stable popularity, TTL for freshness, and protect against scans polluting the cache.

questions.q: How do I design pagination for massive datasets efficiently?
a: Keyset (cursor) pagination over offset, a stable sort key with a tiebreaker, bounded page size, and a plan for results that change between pages.

questions.q: Build idempotency for a write API that clients and your own gateway can both retry.
also: How do I handle idempotency for write APIs?
a: Client-supplied key, atomic claim of the key with the write, stored response for replays, key expiry, and the in-flight duplicate case. Say what you do when the request body differs.

Idempotency key per logical operation, atomically recorded with the write, replayed response on duplicates, a defined behavior for a duplicate that arrives while the first is still running, and key expiry.

questions.q: Where is eventual consistency acceptable in a payments flow, and where is it never acceptable?
also: When do I accept eventual consistency versus strict consistency?
a: Balances and ledger postings need strong guarantees. Notifications, search views and analytics can lag. State the invariant first, then pick the weakest consistency that protects it.
Strict where a violation causes money, safety or legal harm. Eventual where staleness is invisible or recoverable. Decide from the invariant, not from habit.

questions.q: Give users read-your-writes when reads are served from replicas.
also: How do I handle read your own writes in a distributed system?
a: Route a user's reads to the primary for a short window, or carry a log position token and wait for replicas to reach it. Compare cost and complexity.
Sticky reads from the primary after a write, session tokens tracking a replica position, or client-side caching of the just-written value.

questions.q: How do I model consistency levels across services and data stores?
a: Decide per data class: strong for money and inventory, read-your-writes for user-facing state, eventual for derived views. Document the guarantee at each service boundary.

questions.q: How do I reason about CAP trade-offs for a given product requirement?
a: CAP only matters during a partition. For each operation decide whether it must refuse (consistency) or may proceed on stale or divergent data (availability), and what reconciliation follows.

questions.q: Replace a two-phase commit across three services.
also: How do I implement distributed transactions without 2PC pain?
a: Saga with compensations, transactional outbox, idempotent consumers. Be honest about what you give up: isolation. Show how a half-finished saga is visible and recoverable.
Sagas with compensating actions, outbox for reliable event emission, idempotent steps, and clear handling for stuck or partially complete flows.

questions.q: How do I design an outbox and inbox pattern for reliable events?
a: Write the event in the same transaction as the state change, relay it to the broker, and dedupe on the consumer with an inbox table keyed by event id. Cover relay lag and ordering.

questions.q: How do I reconcile divergent data across systems?
a: Pick a source of truth per field, run periodic comparison jobs, classify differences, auto-repair the safe ones, and route the rest for review. Track drift as a metric.

questions.q: Generate unique IDs across regions without a central counter.
also: How do I design id generation that works across regions?
a: Snowflake-style, ULID, UUIDv7. Clock skew, sortability, index locality, and what breaks if a node reuses a worker id.
Time-ordered unique ids (Snowflake, ULID, UUIDv7), per-node identifiers, clock skew handling, and index-friendly ordering. Avoid a global counter on the hot path.

questions.q: Where do Raft, Paxos, quorums and gossip appear in a system you would really build?
also: How do Raft, Paxos, gossip, and quorum based replication actually fit into my design?
a: Coordination and metadata on a consensus log, tunable quorums for data, gossip for membership and failure detection. Show that you use them, not reimplement them.
Explain the guarantee each one provides, what it costs in latency and availability, and where it sits in the design (coordination service, replication layer, membership). Name a real system for each.
Consensus for leader election and metadata, quorum reads and writes for tunable consistency, gossip for membership and failure detection. Use proven implementations.

questions.q: You need a distributed lock so only one worker processes a job. How do you make it actually safe?
a: A distributed lock is only as safe as what happens when the holder stalls. Leases expire, so two processes can believe they hold the lock. Safety comes from fencing tokens that the protected resource checks, or from making the operation idempotent so duplicates don't matter.

questions.q: Can you use timestamps to order events or resolve conflicts across machines?
a: Physical clocks across machines are never perfectly in sync, so timestamps can't be trusted to order events or decide which write is newer. Use a single source of order (a sequencer or leader per key), logical clocks (Lamport, vector or hybrid logical clocks), or merges that don't depend on time.

questions.q: A flash sale has 1,000 units and 500,000 people trying to buy at once. How do you never oversell?
a: Overselling is a concurrency bug; the spike is a load problem. Solve the first with atomic reservations against a single source of truth with expiring holds, and the second with admission control, a waiting room, and moving the hot counter off the main database path.

questions.q: Design a ledger for a payments or lending product. Why double-entry, and what invariants must it enforce?
a: A ledger records every movement of money as immutable, balanced journal entries: each transaction has entries that sum to zero across accounts. Balances are derived from entries, corrections are reversing entries, and posting is idempotent. This gives auditability and makes errors detectable.

questions.q: When is event sourcing with CQRS the right call, and when is it a trap?
a: Event sourcing stores state as an append-only sequence of domain events and derives current state by replay; CQRS separates write models from read models. Together they fit domains where history is central. Applied broadly, they add heavy costs in versioning, projections, consistency and data deletion.

questions.q: List the ways a three-tier service fails under real load before drawing any boxes.
also: What are all the ways my system can fail under real traffic?
a: Slow dependencies, retries, queue growth, GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, bad deploys, clock drift, partial network partitions. Slow is worse than down.
Overload, slow or failing dependencies, resource exhaustion, bad deploys, data corruption, network partitions, cascading retries, and operator error. Group by blast radius.

questions.q: How do I design for graceful degradation instead of hard failure?
a: Rank features by importance, define a fallback for each dependency (cached, default, hidden), and test the degraded modes. Decide in advance what the user sees.

questions.q: The original trigger is gone, but the system stays down. What's happening, and how do you get out of it?
a: A metastable failure is one where a temporary trigger pushes the system into a bad state that a feedback loop then sustains, even after the trigger disappears. Recovery means breaking the loop, usually by drastically reducing load, not waiting or restarting.

questions.q: Your service promises 99.95%, but a critical third-party provider offers only 99.5%. How do you design around it?
a: You can't be more available than your synchronous critical path. If a dependency is less reliable than your target, remove it from the synchronous path, make it redundant with a second provider, degrade gracefully when it's down, or lower your promise.

questions.q: Retries are amplifying an outage. Design retries that do not.
also: How do I implement retries without causing storms and loops?
a: Retry budgets, exponential backoff with jitter, deadline propagation, retry at one layer only, idempotent operations only, and a kill switch.
Capped attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets, deadline propagation, retries at a single layer, and only for idempotent operations.

questions.q: Choose and size circuit breakers, bulkheads and timeouts.
also: How do I design circuit breakers and bulkheads correctly?
a: Timeout below the caller's deadline, bulkhead per dependency, breaker thresholds from observed error rate. Cover half-open probing and fallback behavior.
Breaker opens on error or latency thresholds and probes in half-open state. Bulkheads isolate thread or connection pools per dependency. Tune from measured behavior and test them.

questions.q: Fail over between two regions without split brain.
also: How do I run in multiple regions and fail over cleanly?
a: Single writer per partition, fencing tokens, health-based traffic shifting, data loss window (RPO) and recovery time (RTO) stated up front. Practice the failover, do not just draw it.
Active-active or active-passive, a single writer per data partition, replication lag and loss window stated, health-driven DNS or traffic management, and regular failover drills.

questions.q: How do I design for data center outage scenarios?
a: Spread across zones first, then regions. Know your capacity after losing one site, replicate data with a stated loss window, and keep traffic shifting and runbooks tested.

questions.q: Plan a rollback for a release that has already migrated data.
also: How do I design a rollback strategy for bad releases?
a: Backward compatible schema, feature flags, forward-fix versus rollback decision rule, and data written by the new code that the old code must still read.
Canary and progressive rollout, automatic rollback on SLO regression, backward-compatible schemas, feature flags, and a clear rule for rolling back versus fixing forward.

questions.q: Define SLOs for a lending platform and derive alerts from the error budget.
also: How do I define SLOs and design around them?
a: User-visible indicators such as approval latency and disbursal success. Multi-window burn rate alerts. Link budget exhaustion to a release freeze policy.
Pick user-visible indicators, set targets from user need and cost, track error budget, alert on burn rate, and let budget exhaustion change release behavior.

questions.q: How do I make rebuild from scratch possible if everything is lost?
a: Infrastructure as code, tested backups with restore drills, a replayable event log as source of truth, documented bootstrap order, and a measured recovery time.

questions.q: Design health checks for a service. What should liveness and readiness actually check?
a: Liveness answers 'should this process be restarted?' and must only fail when restarting would help. Readiness answers 'should this instance receive traffic now?'. Neither should cascade a shared dependency failure into mass restarts or removing every instance.

questions.q: Every deploy causes a small spike of errors. How do you shut instances down gracefully?
a: Graceful shutdown is a sequence: stop receiving new traffic, let routing changes propagate, finish in-flight work within a deadline, release resources cleanly, then exit. Skipping any step turns every deploy and scale-in into a burst of user-visible errors.

questions.q: Event-driven or request-response for order placement? Decide and defend it.
also: When do I choose event-driven over request-response?
a: Customer needs an answer now, so the order write is synchronous. Downstream work (fulfilment, notifications) is asynchronous. Say where you need a durable event and where a call is enough.
When producers should not wait or know about consumers, when work can be asynchronous, when many consumers need the same fact, or when you need replay. Not when the caller needs an immediate answer.

questions.q: Exactly-once in practice: what do Kafka and Flink give you, and what do you still own?
also: How do I handle exactly once versus at least once semantics in practice?
a: Idempotent producers, transactions, checkpointed state. The sink and any external side effect still need idempotency. Be precise: exactly-once processing, not exactly-once delivery.

Assume at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent. Use transactional or idempotent producers and checkpointed processing where available, and note that external side effects need their own dedupe.

questions.q: A poison message blocks a partition. Design the handling.
also: How do I avoid processing the same event forever due to poison messages?
a: Bounded retries, retry topics with delay, dead-letter topic with context, alert on DLQ depth, and a safe replay tool. Decide when skipping is acceptable.
Attempt counters, routing to a dead-letter destination after a limit, per-message isolation so one bad record does not block the stream, and alerts for investigation.

questions.q: How do I design dead-letter queues and retry policies?
a: Bounded retries with backoff, delayed retry queues, a dead-letter queue carrying error context, alerting on its depth, and a safe replay path.

questions.q: Keep ordering when you also need parallelism.
also: How do I handle ordering of events when it matters?
a: Key by the entity whose order matters, choose partition count for peak consumers, sequence numbers per key, and what happens during rebalance.
Partition by the key whose order matters, sequence numbers for detecting gaps and duplicates, single consumer per partition, and care during rebalances and retries.

questions.q: Design a scheduler for millions of delayed jobs a day.
also: How do I design a job scheduler for millions of jobs a day?
a: Time-bucketed storage, a sharded poller with leases, at-least-once execution with idempotent jobs, clock skew, backlog catch-up after an outage.
Sharded time-bucketed storage, workers claiming jobs with leases, idempotent job execution, retry with backoff, and recovery of jobs held by crashed workers.

questions.q: How do I track the status of long-running jobs for users?
a: A job record with state, progress and error, returned immediately with an id. Clients poll or subscribe. Make states resumable and make the record the source of truth, not the queue.

questions.q: How do I design a fan-out and fan-in pipeline for heavy computations?
a: Split into idempotent tasks, track completion by counter or barrier, handle partial failure and stragglers, and bound concurrency to protect shared resources.

questions.q: Evolve an event schema without breaking consumers.
also: How do I design an event schema that can evolve safely?
a: Schema registry with compatibility mode, additive changes, tolerant readers, versioned topics only as a last resort, and a deprecation window with consumer inventory.
Schema registry with a compatibility rule, additive-only changes by default, tolerant readers, explicit versioning for breaks, and a plan to retire old versions.

questions.q: Design a home feed: fan-out on write or on read? What about users with millions of followers?
a: Fan-out on write precomputes feeds for fast reads but explodes for accounts with huge followings. Fan-out on read is cheap to write but slow to read. Production feeds use a hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities, and precompute only for active users.

questions.q: Design outgoing webhooks to customers' endpoints. What happens when their endpoint is slow or down?
a: Webhooks are at-least-once, asynchronous deliveries to systems you don't control. Make delivery durable and retried, isolate endpoints from each other, sign payloads, include ids for deduplication, and give customers visibility and replay.

questions.q: Compute per-minute metrics from a stream where events arrive late and out of order. How do windows and watermarks work?
a: Correct streaming aggregates use event time, not arrival time. Watermarks estimate how far event time has progressed so windows can close; allowed lateness lets late events update results; and anything later than that is handled explicitly, not silently dropped.

questions.q: How many Kafka partitions should a topic have, and why do consumer rebalances keep stalling processing?
a: Partition count sets the ceiling on consumer parallelism and affects ordering, so choose it from throughput needs with growth headroom, not as 'as many as possible'. Rebalances pause consumption; reduce them with cooperative rebalancing, static group membership and correct timeout tuning.

questions.q: Draw service boundaries for a lending platform: origination, underwriting, servicing, collections.
also: How do I define clear boundaries between services?
a: Bound by data ownership and change rate, not by nouns. Decide which data is copied by event and which is queried live. Show where a loan's state machine lives.
One owner per piece of data, interfaces that match business capabilities, low coupling on change, and a test: can a team ship without coordinating with others?

questions.q: Design a gateway that can evolve independently of the services behind it.
also: How do I design a gateway that can evolve independently of services?
a: Keep it thin: routing, auth, limits, observability. No business logic. Config-driven routes, canary support, and its own failure budget.
Thin gateway with routing, auth and limits only, declarative configuration, versioned routes, and no knowledge of service internals.

questions.q: Version a public API when you cannot force clients to upgrade.
also: How do I design versioning for public APIs?
How do I design APIs so they can evolve without breaking clients?
a: Additive changes by default, explicit versions for breaking ones, a support policy with dates, usage telemetry per version, and contract tests.
Additive changes within a version, a new version for breaking changes, a published support policy, usage metrics per version, and clear deprecation dates.
Additive changes only, optional fields with defaults, tolerant readers, explicit versioning for breaks, and contract tests against real client usage.

questions.q: Deprecate an endpoint safely.
also: How do I design a safe deprecation process?
a: Find real callers from logs, announce with dates, add Sunset headers, brown-out in staging then production, and keep a path for stragglers.
Identify callers from telemetry, announce with dates, warn in responses, run brownouts, support stragglers, and only then remove.

questions.q: How do I design for backward compatibility with older clients?
a: Support-window policy, version telemetry, feature negotiation, and server-side shims for the oldest supported clients. Know when you can finally stop supporting one.

questions.q: How do I handle breaking change scenarios with minimal disruption?
a: Run old and new in parallel, migrate clients with tooling and dates, monitor who still calls the old path, and offer a rollback during the cutover.

questions.q: How do I design for backward compatibility when schemas change?
a: Additive fields, defaults for missing values, never reuse or repurpose a field, readers that ignore unknown fields, and compatibility checks in CI.

questions.q: Design per-tenant rate limits that do not punish well-behaved bursty clients.
also: How do I design tenant-level rate limits and quotas?
How do I design rate limiting that does not break good users?
a: Token bucket with burst allowance, shared counters in a fast store, local approximation to cut round trips, clear 429 responses, and tiered quotas.
Limits per tenant and per plan, burst allowance, shared counters in a fast store, fair sharing under contention, and visibility so tenants see their usage.
Token bucket with burst headroom, limits per identity rather than per IP where possible, clear 429 responses with retry hints, and separate limits for abusive and normal traffic.

questions.q: One request fans out to five services and two fail. What do you return?
also: How do I handle partial failures in multi-service calls?
a: Classify calls as required or optional, return degraded results with a marker, set per-call timeouts, never block the whole response on the slowest optional call.
Timeouts per call, required versus optional dependencies, degraded responses, compensations for completed steps, and idempotency so retries are safe.

questions.q: REST, gRPC or GraphQL: how do you choose for a given API?
a: Choose an API style by who consumes it and how: REST for broad, cacheable, public interfaces; gRPC for typed, efficient internal communication and streaming; GraphQL for client-driven aggregation across many backends. Each has distinct costs in caching, security and operations.

questions.q: Push updates to clients in real time: polling, long polling, server-sent events or WebSockets?
a: Choose by direction and frequency: polling for infrequent updates, long polling as a fallback, server-sent events for one-way server push, WebSockets for frequent two-way messaging. The hard part is the backend: stateful connection servers, routing messages to the right connection, and handling reconnects.

questions.q: Design a bulk API that creates 10,000 records in one request. What happens when some of them fail?
a: Bulk APIs must define partial success explicitly: per-item status and errors, per-item idempotency so retries are safe, size limits, and asynchronous processing for large batches. All-or-nothing transactions are only appropriate for small batches that must be atomic.

questions.q: Sessions or JWTs for authentication? How do you log a user out everywhere or revoke a stolen token?
a: Server-side sessions are easy to revoke but need a lookup per request; JWTs avoid the lookup but can't be revoked before expiry without extra state. The standard compromise is short-lived access tokens with server-side, rotating refresh tokens, and storing tokens where scripts can't steal them.

questions.q: How should internal services authenticate and authorise calls to each other?
a: Internal calls need real authentication and authorisation: each workload has a short-lived cryptographic identity, connections use mutual TLS, services authorise callers per endpoint, and end-user identity is propagated in signed tokens rather than trusted headers.

questions.q: Design authorisation for a multi-tenant API. How do you stop users accessing other people's resources?
a: Authorisation has to be enforced where the resource lives, for every object access, not just at the edge. Choose a model that fits (RBAC for roles, ABAC for attribute rules, relationship-based for sharing), centralise the policy logic, and test explicitly for cross-tenant and cross-user access.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets, and rotate a database password or API key without downtime?
a: Store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager with access control and audit, deliver them to workloads at runtime, and rotate using an overlap period where both old and new credentials are valid. Better still, replace static secrets with short-lived, automatically issued credentials.

questions.q: "Is the data encrypted?" What does a real answer about encryption at rest, in transit and key management look like?
a: Encryption only helps against the threats it's designed for. Storage encryption covers lost disks and backups; application-level field encryption protects sensitive data from people and systems with database access. Both depend on key management: keys in a KMS or HSM, envelope encryption, least-privilege access, rotation and audit.

questions.q: How do you handle card numbers and other highly sensitive data without putting your whole platform in compliance scope?
a: The best way to protect highly sensitive data is to not hold it. Tokenisation replaces card numbers or national ids with tokens everywhere except a small, isolated vault, ideally run by a payment provider, which shrinks compliance scope and breach impact.

questions.q: Attackers are trying millions of leaked passwords against your login. How do you protect accounts without locking out real users?
a: Credential stuffing uses leaked username and password pairs at scale, distributed across many IPs. Defend in layers: make guessing expensive and slow, detect automation, stop known-breached passwords, require stronger factors when risk is high, and watch for anomalies, without hard lockouts that attackers can weaponise.

questions.q: Design an audit log that auditors, security and support can trust.
a: Audit logs are a separate product from debugging logs: complete, structured records of who did what to which resource, when, from where and why, stored so they can't be silently altered, retained for the required period, and accessible under strict control.

questions.q: What should each layer log, and what must never be logged?
also: What should I log at each layer, and what should I never log?
a: Structured logs with a request id at every layer. Never log secrets, tokens, full card numbers or personal data. Sampling for high-volume paths and retention by sensitivity.
Structured logs with correlation ids, entry and exit of requests, errors with context, and decisions. Never secrets, tokens, full payment data or unnecessary personal data.

questions.q: Trace a request across 50 services without a runaway bill.
also: How do I design tracing across 50+ microservices?
a: Context propagation everywhere, tail-based sampling that keeps errors and slow traces, span attributes that are queryable, and a budget per team.
Standard context propagation, consistent span naming, tail-based sampling to keep slow and failed traces, and links from metrics and logs to traces.

questions.q: Alert on user pain, not on noise.
also: How do I design alerting that catches real issues but avoids noise?
a: Page on symptoms such as error rate and latency against SLOs, ticket on causes. Every page needs an owner and a runbook link. Delete alerts that nobody acted on.
Alert on user-facing symptoms and SLO burn, attach runbooks, deduplicate and group, review noisy alerts regularly, and delete the ones that never lead to action.

questions.q: How do I design metrics that actually tell me system health?
a: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation per service and per dependency, with histograms rather than averages and business metrics alongside technical ones.

questions.q: How do I design dashboards that help during incidents?
a: One top-level health view, then drill-down by service and dependency. Put symptoms first, show deploy markers, and keep the layout the same across services.

questions.q: p50 is flat but p99 doubled. How do you debug it?
also: How do I debug high tail latency in a distributed system?
a: Look for queueing, GC, noisy neighbors, a slow shard, retries, lock contention. Compare by instance, endpoint and dependency. Use exemplars to jump from a metric to a trace.
Compare percentiles by instance, endpoint and dependency, look for queueing, GC, retries and hot shards, and use traces to find the slow span. Hedged requests can mask but not fix it.

questions.q: Rehearse failure before production does it for you.
also: How do I simulate failures before they hit production?
a: Game days, dependency fault injection, region evacuation drills, restore-from-backup tests. Start in staging with a hypothesis and a stop condition.
Fault injection for dependencies and infrastructure, game days, load and soak tests, and restore drills, starting with a hypothesis and a clear abort condition.

questions.q: Write a runbook the on-call engineer can follow at 3 a.m.
also: How do I design runbooks so on-call engineers can act fast?
a: Symptom first, then checks in order, then safe actions with exact commands, then when to escalate. Tested by someone who did not write it.
Start from the alert, give ordered checks, exact commands, safe mitigations, escalation paths, and keep them tested and reviewed after incidents.

questions.q: You're incident commander for a major outage. What do you do in the first 15 minutes?
a: The incident commander's job is coordination, not debugging: establish roles and communication, keep the team focused on restoring service rather than finding root cause, make decisions with incomplete information, and keep stakeholders informed on a predictable cadence.

questions.q: Blue-green, canary or rolling deploys: what does each protect you from, and what doesn't it?
a: Deployment strategies trade blast radius, speed and cost. Rolling replaces instances gradually; blue-green switches all traffic between two environments; canary exposes a small slice first and expands on healthy metrics. None of them protect against incompatible data changes.

questions.q: A one-line config change took down every region. How should dynamic configuration be rolled out?
a: Dynamic configuration, feature flags, routing rules and data files can change the behaviour of every server at once, so they need the same safety as code: review, validation, staged rollout across failure domains, automatic rollback and fail-safe loading.

questions.q: Autoscaling is enabled, yet the service still falls over during spikes. Why?
a: Autoscaling reacts in minutes to the metric you choose, so it fails when the metric isn't the bottleneck, the spike is faster than scaling, new instances start cold, or more instances overwhelm a shared dependency. Combine it with headroom, the right signals, warm-up and load shedding.

questions.q: You moved an API to serverless functions and the relational database started failing under load. What went wrong?
a: Serverless functions scale out to many concurrent instances, each with its own connections, which overwhelms relational databases built for a modest number of long-lived connections. Use connection proxies, concurrency caps and connection reuse, or data stores designed for this access pattern.

questions.q: Leadership wants active-active multi-region. What does it really cost, and when isn't it worth it?
a: Active-active means serving production traffic from multiple regions at once, which can deliver very high availability and lower latency, but at the cost of roughly doubled infrastructure, complex data replication or partitioning, and much harder operations. Justify it with the cost of downtime, not as a default.

questions.q: Estimate QPS, storage and bandwidth from daily active users. What are the common estimation traps?
a: Good estimates make every assumption explicit: users to actions, actions to requests (including fan-out), average to peak, items to bytes (including metadata, indexes and replication), and today to the planning horizon. Round numbers are fine; missing factors aren't.

questions.q: Design retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over company documents. Where does it usually go wrong?
a: RAG quality is mostly retrieval quality. Chunk by document structure, combine keyword and semantic search, rerank, filter by the user's permissions, keep the index fresh, ground answers with citations, and measure retrieval and answer quality with an evaluation set.

questions.q: Choose and size a vector index for 100 million embeddings. What trade-offs matter?
a: Vector search at scale uses approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes that trade recall, latency, memory and update cost. Size memory explicitly, choose the index type to fit, measure recall against exact search, and design metadata filtering so it doesn't silently destroy result quality.

questions.q: Your LLM feature is slow and expensive. How do you reduce latency and cost?
a: LLM cost and latency scale with tokens processed and generated, and with serving efficiency. Reduce input and output tokens, route requests to the smallest model that meets quality, stream to cut perceived latency, reuse work with caching, and batch where latency allows, all measured against a quality bar.

questions.q: Can you cache LLM responses? What about semantic caching?
a: LLM outputs can be cached, but the cache key must capture everything that affects the answer: model, prompt version, parameters, retrieved context and user-specific data. Exact-match and prefix caching are safe; semantic caching saves more but risks wrong or leaked answers and needs strict scoping.

questions.q: Your product depends on an external LLM API. How do you handle rate limits, outages and slow responses?
a: External LLM APIs have rate limits on requests and tokens, variable latency and occasional outages. Treat them like any critical third-party dependency: centralised quota management, prioritisation, timeouts, careful retries, pre-tested fallbacks with their own prompts, and degraded experiences when nothing is available.

questions.q: How do you safely change a prompt or upgrade the model behind an LLM feature?
a: Treat prompts and model versions like code: version them, test them against representative evaluation sets with clear graders, roll them out gradually behind flags, and monitor quality, safety, cost and latency online with the ability to roll back.

questions.q: Your LLM feature can call tools and read user content. How do you defend against prompt injection and abuse?
a: LLMs can't reliably distinguish instructions from data, so any untrusted content they read can manipulate them. Defend by design: least-privilege tools, enforce authorisation outside the model, require confirmation for consequential actions, treat model output as untrusted input, filter and monitor, and rate-limit abuse.

questions.q: How do I design something MVP-first that can still grow?
a: Make the cheapest design that satisfies today's load, but keep the seams that are expensive to add later: identifiers, data ownership, API contracts and observability.

questions.q: How do I choose between building a platform and a one-off service?
a: Build a platform when three or more teams need the same capability and the interface is stable. Otherwise ship the one-off and extract later from real usage.

questions.q: How do I design for cost visibility and optimization from day one?
a: Tag every resource by team and service, expose cost per request or per tenant, set budgets and alerts, and review the top spenders on a schedule.

questions.q: Decide what to buy and what to build.
also: How do I decide what to buy versus what to build?
a: Build what differentiates you and what you must control. Buy commodity. Count integration, lock-in, data egress and the people cost of running either.
Build what differentiates you or needs deep control. Buy commodity capability. Weigh lock-in, integration cost, data portability, and the ongoing cost of operating either choice.

questions.q: How do I design systems that multiple teams can safely extend?
a: Clear extension points, stable contracts, isolation so one team's plugin cannot take down others, and ownership documented per component.

questions.q: How do I plan for data residency and regional regulations?
a: Tag data by jurisdiction, pin storage and processing to regions, control cross-region replication and logs, and design deletion and access requests per region.

questions.q: How do I design to support experiments such as A/B tests and flags cleanly?
a: Central flag service with stable user bucketing, exposure logging, kill switches, and a cleanup process for dead flags. Keep experiment logic out of business code paths where possible.

questions.q: How do I design migration paths when the legacy system cannot just die?
a: Strangler pattern: route slices of traffic to the new system, keep both in sync during the overlap, migrate data by domain, and define an exit criterion for the old system.

questions.q: Defend a design trade-off to a skeptical architect in five minutes.
also: How do I defend trade-offs to a sceptical architect?
a: State the constraint, the options you rejected and why, what would change your mind, and how you will find out cheaply if you are wrong.
State requirements and constraints, show alternatives with costs, say what you are giving up, and name the signal that would make you reverse the decision.

questions.q: Review a peer's design deeply and still be easy to work with.
also: How do I review someone else's design deeply but respectfully?
a: Ask questions that expose assumptions, separate blocking concerns from preferences, propose an alternative when you object, and credit what is good.
Understand the goal first, ask questions about failure and scale, separate must-fix from preference, suggest alternatives, and acknowledge what is solid.

questions.q: How do I explain my design to a junior developer so they truly get it?
a: Start from the problem and one request path, add pieces only as the problem demands them, use a single diagram, and check understanding by asking them to predict a failure.

questions.q: How do you tell when a design is over-engineered?
also: How do I know when a design is over-engineered?
a: Components with no current requirement behind them, flexibility nobody has asked for, more moving parts than people to run them.
Complexity without a current requirement, abstractions with one user, more services than teams, and anything you cannot explain the need for in a sentence.

questions.q: How do you tell when a design is dangerously under-engineered?
also: How do I know when a design is dangerously under-engineered?
a: No answer for the failure you can name, no way to roll back, no capacity numbers, one person who understands it.
No failure handling for known risks, no capacity estimate, no rollback or recovery path, unclear ownership, and a single point of failure on a critical path.

questions.q: How do I simplify a complex design without losing guarantees?
a: List the guarantees that must hold, remove components that do not protect one, merge things that always change together, and prove the invariants still hold.

questions.q: How do I design for boring reliability instead of cleverness?
a: Choose proven components, minimize moving parts, prefer simple failure modes, and spend novelty budget only where it creates real advantage.

questions.q: How do I decide what not to build into a system?
a: Tie each feature to a present requirement or measured risk, defer what is cheap to add later, and write the non-goals down.

questions.q: How do I design so that mistakes are cheap, not catastrophic?
a: Small blast radius, progressive rollout, reversible changes, backups and restore tests, feature flags, and guardrails on destructive operations.

questions.q: Write a design doc that is still useful in three years.
also: How do I write a design doc that survives 3 years of evolution?
a: Context and constraints, alternatives considered, decisions with reasons, non-goals, and open questions. The reasons age better than the diagrams.
Record context, goals and non-goals, alternatives considered, decisions and their reasons, and known risks. Date it, link follow-ups, and keep diagrams simple.

questions.q: How do I design systems that can be owned by teams, not heroes?
a: Documented runbooks, shared on-call, boring technology, clear ownership boundaries, and no component only one person understands.

questions.q: You need 15 teams to migrate off a deprecated platform, and you don't manage any of them. How do you drive it?
a: Driving work across teams you don't manage is about reducing their cost and increasing their reasons: make migration nearly free with tooling and hands-on help, explain the benefit in their terms, create visible momentum, and reserve escalation for the end.

questions.q: A VP wants a launch in six weeks with a design you believe is risky. How do you push back?
a: Pushing back works when it gives decision-makers better choices, not just objections. Understand the goal behind the deadline, quantify the risk, offer concrete options trading scope, time and risk, and once a decision is made, commit and record it.

questions.q: Your change caused a production incident. What do you do and say, during and after?
a: Own it quickly and plainly, prioritise mitigation, communicate impact honestly, and then fix the system that allowed the mistake, not just your own carefulness. Blameless postmortems work only if the person who made the change is open about it.

questions.q: How do you get tech debt prioritised against feature work?
a: Tech debt gets prioritised when it's expressed as business cost and risk, tied to goals people already care about, and delivered incrementally with visible results. Treat it like a product backlog with a return on investment, not a moral argument.

questions.q: One team wants a different database or framework that suits them better. When do you standardise, and when do you allow local choices?
a: Standardisation reduces organisational costs (operations, security, hiring, shared tooling); local optimisation captures fit-for-purpose benefits. Decide by who bears the cost of variety, and make exceptions deliberate, owned and documented rather than forbidden or invisible.

questions.q: You led a major architecture change. How do you prove it worked?
a: Decide what success means before the change: specific outcome metrics tied to the problem it was meant to solve, with baselines. Measure after rollout over comparable periods, account for confounding changes and costs, and report results honestly, including disappointments.

questions.q: Integrate a card payment provider: authorise, capture, refund, with webhooks. What does your payment state machine look like?
a: Payments are long-running, asynchronous processes with uncertain outcomes. Model them as an explicit state machine, use idempotency keys on every provider call, treat timeouts as 'unknown' to be resolved, process webhooks idempotently and in a way that tolerates reordering, and reconcile against provider reports.

questions.q: Design refunds, reversals and chargebacks. What makes them harder than the original payment?
a: Money flowing back is a separate lifecycle, not an undo. Refunds (merchant-initiated), reversals (voiding before settlement) and chargebacks (customer bank-initiated disputes) each need their own records, states, ledger entries and handling of funds that may already have moved onward.

questions.q: How do you represent money, rounding and multiple currencies correctly?
a: Money is an amount plus a currency, stored as an integer in the currency's minor unit, with rounding applied deliberately at specified steps using a specified mode. Splits must allocate remainders so totals reconcile, and currency conversion records rate, source and timestamp.

questions.q: Design daily interest accrual and end-of-day processing for millions of loans.
a: Daily accrual is a ledger operation per loan per business date: deterministic, idempotent and recorded as entries, not balance updates. Run it as a partitioned, resumable batch tied to an explicit business date, handle missed days and backdated events, and reconcile totals.

questions.q: Design KYC onboarding and ongoing AML monitoring for a fintech.
a: KYC and AML are continuous, risk-based processes, not a one-time check: verify identity at onboarding proportionate to risk, screen against sanctions and PEP lists continuously, monitor transactions for suspicious patterns, route alerts to analysts through case management, and keep auditable records of every decision.

questions.q: Design a real-time bidder that must respond to ad auctions within about 100 ms at very high request rates.
a: In real-time bidding, latency is correctness: a late answer loses the auction. Keep the decision path in memory with precomputed campaign indexes and user segments, enforce a strict internal deadline with no-bid fallbacks, and handle budgets and logging asynchronously.

questions.q: Thousands of bidders spend from the same campaign budget. How do you pace spend and avoid overspending?
a: Budget control in adtech is a distributed rate-limiting problem with delayed feedback. Split budgets into allowances leased to bidders, account for in-flight bids whose cost isn't known yet, pace spend over time rather than spending as fast as possible, and bound overspend explicitly.

questions.q: Enforce "show this ad to a user at most 3 times a day" across billions of impressions.
a: Frequency capping is a high-volume, latency-critical counting problem with delayed signals. Keep counters in a fast key-value store with expiring windows, read them in the bid path with tight timeouts, update them from impression streams, and accept bounded overcapping instead of strict global consistency.

questions.q: Count impressions and clicks for billing, filter fraud, and attribute conversions that happen days later.
a: Ad metrics serve two masters: fast approximate numbers for pacing and dashboards, and exact, audited numbers for billing. Deduplicate by event id, filter invalid traffic, handle late events and attribution windows, and produce billable figures from a reproducible batch pipeline reconciled with partners.

questions.q: The cart showed one price, checkout charged another, and a single-use coupon was used twice. How do you design checkout and promotions?
a: Checkout must charge exactly what the customer agreed to. Freeze a priced quote (items, prices, discounts, tax, shipping) with an expiry, evaluate promotions with deterministic rules, reserve limited redemptions atomically, and confirm or release them with the order.

questions.q: Search results show products that are out of stock or have the wrong price. How do you keep catalogue search fresh?
a: Search indexes are derived data and will lag. Keep lag small with event-driven incremental indexing, treat volatile fields like stock and price specially (partial updates or query-time overlays), rebuild periodically for correctness, and always verify against the source of truth at decision points.

questions.q: A marketplace takes payment from buyers and pays out to many sellers, minus fees. How do you design split payments and payouts?
a: Marketplace money flows through a ledger: buyer payments credit seller balances minus fees, funds become available after holds, payouts move available balances to sellers on a schedule, and refunds or chargebacks debit balances. This decouples order events from bank transfers and makes recovery possible.

questions.q: Fake listings and fake reviews are hurting trust in your marketplace. How do you design fraud detection?
a: Marketplace fraud is adversarial and evolves, so defend in layers: score risk at each key action using rules, models and relationship signals, apply graduated responses rather than binary bans, route uncertain cases to humans, and feed outcomes back to adapt.

questions.q: Match riders to drivers (or orders to couriers) in real time, including when demand far exceeds supply.
a: Dispatch is an optimisation problem under latency constraints. Gather candidates via geospatial indexes, score by real ETA and other costs, match requests and drivers in short batches to improve global outcomes, guarantee each driver gets one offer at a time, and manage shortages explicitly with queues, wider searches and pricing.

questions.q: Hundreds of thousands of drivers send GPS updates every few seconds. How do you ingest, store and serve them?
a: Location updates are high-volume, short-lived data. Keep only the latest position per driver in an in-memory, sharded geospatial index for real-time queries, stream all updates to durable cheap storage for history, and clean noisy GPS before it drives decisions.

questions.q: Design surge pricing and ETA estimates. How do you keep them fast, fair and consistent with what the customer is charged?
a: Dynamic pricing works from aggregated, smoothed supply and demand per area and time window, not per request. Show customers a locked upfront quote that's honoured, compute ETAs with a mix of cached and routed estimates, and measure both against real outcomes.

questions.q: Show customers accurate stock and delivery promises when inventory sits across many warehouses and stores.
a: Available-to-promise (ATP) is not on-hand stock. It's sellable quantity per location after reservations and safety buffers, plus inbound supply that arrives in time, filtered by locations that can meet the promised date. Orders reserve against specific locations, and physical counts continually correct the numbers.

questions.q: Warehouse scanners and delivery devices go offline, then upload events hours later and out of order. How do you keep shipment state correct?
a: Edge devices produce events offline that arrive late, duplicated and out of order. Give every event a unique id and device time and sequence, ingest idempotently, derive current state from the ordered event history with a state machine that accepts late events, and flag genuine conflicts for review.

questions.q: You integrate with dozens of carriers and suppliers via APIs, files and EDI. How do you keep data flowing and correct?
a: Partner integrations are unreliable, heterogeneous and slow to change. Isolate them behind an integration layer with a canonical internal model, per-partner adapters, durable asynchronous delivery, raw message archives, monitoring per partner, and regular reconciliation to catch what fell through the cracks.

questions.q: Plan delivery routes for thousands of drivers each day, and adjust when things change during the day.
a: Route optimisation is an NP-hard problem solved with heuristics under time limits. Plan in batch before the day starts, partitioned by region, then repair routes incrementally as orders, traffic and failures change, preferring stability for drivers over theoretical optimality.

questions.q: Thousands of students submit an exam or assignment in the last minute before the deadline. How do you make sure no submission is lost?
a: Deadline spikes are predictable and extreme. Make the submit path a tiny, durable, timestamped write that can absorb the burst, defer all heavy processing to queues, autosave work continuously so nothing is lost, and define fair handling of late or failed submissions caused by the platform.

questions.q: Run timed online exams fairly: enforce time limits, randomise questions and resist cheating.
a: Exam integrity can't rely on the client. The server owns start and end times, delivers questions progressively from randomised pools, records answers as they're given, applies accommodations per student, and treats proctoring signals as evidence for human review.

questions.q: Design live online classes with interactive video for small groups and lectures for thousands.
a: Real-time video architecture depends on group size and interactivity. Peer-to-peer works for two or three people; selective forwarding units (SFUs) handle interactive groups; broadcast via CDN-based streaming handles large audiences, with a few presenters interactive and everyone else watching with a few seconds of delay.

questions.q: Learners use the app offline on multiple devices. How do you sync progress and grades without losing or corrupting data?
a: Offline multi-device sync works best when devices record immutable events rather than overwrite state. Events sync idempotently, merge with rules that are order-independent (union of completed lessons, best score), and anything that matters for grades is validated server-side.
